the pathogenesis of most primary liver tumors is not yet completely understood.

the pathogenesis of liver carcinogenesis induced by chemicals is a multistage process, involving a number of cellular alterations, which are not necessarily restricted to the hepatocytes, and which may be initiated by various carcinogens, acting by different mechanisms [7].
hepatocarcino-gens may act as tumor initiators and tumor promoters in the hepatocyte and as tumor promoters in the bile ductular cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

hepatocarcino-genesis involves a multistep process in which the initiation of neoplastic changes is followed by a series of progressive alterations of the cell phenotype, resulting in the formation of benign and malignant tumors [7, 8, 9].
the liver has a high capacity for regeneration.

carcinogens may induce tumors in the rat liver by at least three different mechanisms: (1) by direct action on hepatocytes, which leads to the formation of neoplastic nodules; (2) by direct action or indirect effects on bile ductules, which leads to cholangiofibroma; and (3) by direct action, indirect effects, or both, on perisinusoidal or sinusoidal cells, which leads to hemangioendo-thelioma and angiosarcoma
The main takeaway from our work is that
carcinogenesis of the liver may be viewed as an interaction between the carcinogen and various cell types in the liver, which are altered by the carcinogenic agent in different ways.
the liver is a very sensitive organ, which responds to a wide range of chemical and physical carcinogens.
the liver is a very heterogeneous organ, and the various types of target cells may respond differently to the same carcinogen.
